title: Project-Based Learning & Literacy
before:
Project-Based Learning and Literacy

Project-based learning (PBL) and other models, such as play-, problem-, or place-based, are powerful instructional models that engage students in the community around them.  Embedding literacy instruction into PBL is aligned with reading science and can be a powerful combination.  The following module seeks to connect educators with PBL practices that support literacy instruction.  In this module, you will find:

 

  • a definition of project-based learning
  • a connection between foundational literacy and PBL
  • PBL literacy moves based on the Active View of Reading

Literacy Foundations & the Active View of Reading

When we think of foundational literacy, we often think of skills and strategies all readers need to be successful readers.  The following video explains the Structure of Knowledge and the Structure of Process. The purpose is to show educators how foundational skills can be embedded into project-based learning.

Language Comprehension

One of the most powerful instructional moves to support literacy is activating prior knowledge and building background knowledge.  Prior knowledge is everything a student knows about a topic and may be tied to their culture.  For example, students may have prior knowledge about holidays that they celebrate.  That knowledge will help them comprehend holiday books.

notes: 470 words with no section headers at all — the biggest single improvement available here.

decisions.label: Set an over-long heading as the paragraph it is
decisions.why: 2 headings run past 100 characters — the longest here is 362. "When we think of foundational literacy, we often think o…" is body text that was set as a heading to make it stand out, so it is announced as a section of the page and, at h2, written into the contents list as a link. It becomes a paragraph. Any anchor on it is kept, so existing links still land, and not a word changes.

decisions.label: Rebuild the heading outline
decisions.why: 1 heading sits at a level the page never opens — "Project-Based Learning and Literacy" is an h3 with no h2 above it, so it is neither announced nor styled as the sub-section it is. Each heading moves to one level below whatever encloses it.

decisions.label: Turn the headings into section headers
decisions.why: 1 heading is plain text where every other page uses a section header, so the page reads as one continuous wall instead of parts.

decisions.label: Write the email addresses the same way
decisions.why: 1 address is shown in whatever case it was typed in. The house form capitalises each name and leaves a middle initial in lower case — kathy.bertini@maine.gov → Kathy.Bertini@maine.gov. Only the first letter of each part changes, so a name that spells itself LaBreck keeps doing so.

decisions.label: Draw a closing link as the action it is
decisions.why: 1 passage ends with a paragraph holding nothing but a link — the thing the passage was leading up to. Set as running text it looks like any other link in the sentence above it. The site already has one way of drawing an action, so it takes that. The words do not change.

decisions.label: Set a job title the way the rest of the site does
decisions.why: 1 job title sits in plain text under the person's name, where 186 elsewhere on the site are in italics — so the same contact block is drawn two ways depending on the page, and the title runs into the name above it. The standard here is the site's own, not a preference: two thirds of these blocks already do it. No word changes.

decisions.label: Remove the first section header
decisions.why: "Project-Based Learning and Literacy" repeats the page title, so the reader is told the same thing twice before any content.

decisions.label: Use this paragraph as the page description
decisions.why: It is the page’s own opening paragraph, moved into the banner rather than rewritten.

decisions.label: Bring every heading up to h3 or above
decisions.why: 15 headings sat at h4 or deeper inside a card, a callout, a contact block or an accordion panel — components the outline walk leaves alone because they label a thing rather than a section. A reader using a screen reader still hears the level, so a fourth-level title inside a page that only goes to three is announced as belonging to a level that does not exist. Each is styled by its class and its position rather than its number, so nothing changes on screen.
